data.title: MAS explores AI agent protocol and tokenisation framework
data.description:
MAS is setting up a sandbox to test AI agents and programmable money for corporate treasury and payments.

The Monetary Authority of Singapore (MAS) will further explore artificial intelligence (AI) agents and tokenisation, setting out plans for a new agent verification protocol, a new sandbox, and updated tokenisation guides.

Whilst adoption of AI agents are still in the early stages, it has the potential to scale rapidly as the industry realizes that it can cut costs and ramp up speed of search and comparison, optimisation and decisions, negotiations and execution, said Chia Der Jiun, managing director of MAS, said in his keynote speech for Day 2 of the Singapore Fintech Festival (SFF) on 19 November.

Chia identified AI agents and tokenisation as the two transformative forces in finance.

“We do not know how quickly agentic transactions will grow, but it is likely that the future will be a mix of the human economy and a new agent economy,” Chia said.

MAS said that it will work to develop a common protocol to verify agents’ representation and mandate, as well as a sandbox to explore AI agents and programmable money, Chia said.

“The two initiatives I've highlighted, common protocols for agent transactions and the sandbox for agentic money, will be important building blocks for the future of agentic transactions,” Chia said.

The common Know-Your-Agent protocol will require customers and financial institutions to exchange information about the agent’s identity, representation, authority, mandate it operates under, and provenance.

MAS believes that this will give financial institutions the information needed to determine the terms and the scope of permission that the agents hold, Chia said.

MAS is also setting up a sandbox with the Future of Finance Institute, bringing together AI agents and programmable money for corporate treasury management and payments services, he said.

Chia recognized that AI can sharply reduce information asymmetries, reduce search and information costs in economic decisions, and enable more dynamic and continuous pricing.

For businesses, agents can automate procurement, inventory management, and other routine commercial decisions, he said.

Tokenised collateral and digital money
Chia said that MAS will work with the industry to onboard and tokenise other commonly used collateral, including foreign government securities and money market funds.

Chia announced the launch of the Guardian Tokenised Collateral Framework, which sets out the operational requirements across the collateral life cycle, including eligibility, custody, valuation, return, and enforcement.

“We are updating the guide on tokenisation of capital markets products to further clarify the regulatory and risk management requirements,” Chia said, adding that they are also working with local legal professionals to clarify issues relating to the tokenization of capital markets products.

These efforts build on MAS’ earlier issue of $100m in tokenised bills, announced by Chia during the 2025 edition of SFF.
https://sbr.com.sg/news/singapore-trial-tokenised-mas-bills-using-central-bank-digital-currency

Chia also outlined various initiatives and new frameworks in Singapore relating to tokenisation, stablecoins, and central bank digital currencies (CBDCs), including the rebranding of SGD Test Net to the SG Ledger, a settlement platform for tokenised assets, forms of digital money, and ledgers.

MAS also released the Bloom Field Guide on 19 November, which details practical considerations for deploying digital money in various cases.

Chia said that MAS tested mechanisms to settle and verify settlement conditions across separate central bank systems with the Bank of England, the Bank of Thailand, and Deutsche Bundesbank.

“This is our approach: collaborate with the industry to lay the foundations and prepare the building blocks, so that the industry can scale where there are commercially compelling use cases,” Chia said.

Chia sees the future of finance as an interoperable ecosystem involving AI agents, financial institutions, and digital money.

“Businesses, financial institutions, financial infrastructure operators will have to adapt to serving both human customers and agents,” he said.

Chia said that financial institutions will have to strengthen their value proposition, and potentially consider whether limits are needed on agent-instructed transactions to manage risk.

Regulators will have to consider the implication for financial stability as agentic use in financial markets and money movements expand.

“Importantly, consumers and businesses need to retain meaningful control over the objectives, mandate, and actions of their agents. Autonomy has to be bounded,” Chia said.

data.title: Fraud rate drops 36% but attacks grow more complex: study
data.description:
Deepfake fraud fell 37%, the second-largest drop in Asia-Pacific after China.

Singapore’s fraud rate dropped 36% year on year (YoY) to 1%, according to a Sumsub study released on 18 November.

Deepfake fraud also fell 37% YoY, the second-largest decline in the Asia-Pacific (APAC) region, behind only China at 59%.

However, Sumsub said attacks are growing more complex. Singapore’s fraud complexity index (FCI) rose 9% to 2.13 points, above the 2.09 APAC average.

APAC topped the six regions in the report, accounting for 33% of fraud networks and close to a million confirmed fraud attempts globally.

Sumsub said regulators in Singapore are shifting responsibility for scam payments and mule accounts to institutions that send, receive or facilitate these transactions, and are building new ways to share fraud intelligence.

Singapore recently rolled out several laws against fraud, including the Protection from Scams Act and the Scams (Countermeasures) and Other Matters Act 2026. A National Scams List was also released to support information exchange on suspicious scam accounts.

Sumsub said APAC businesses suffer from external fraud (42%), followed by scam-induced payments (40%). Amongst consumers, 79% experienced fraud in the past 12 months, with half of victims losing money and 51% recovering none.

data.title: UOB explores A*STAR's multilingual AI for client calls
data.description:
It can interpret questions and concerns across different languages and accents.

UOB is exploring the use of an artificial intelligence (AI)-powered multilingual customer call solution to enhance customer engagement across ASEAN languages and markets.

The bank said it looks to apply the solution, powered by A*STAR's Multimodal Empathetic Reasoning and Learning in One Network (MERaLiON) model, to help relationship managers (RMs) understand, engage, and advise customers in Singapore, Malaysia, Thailand, Indonesia, and Vietnam.

The first phase will be done through Project AURA, the bank’s strategic programme to deploy advanced AI at scale and build an AI-fluent culture.

The solution, called the Compliance Intelligence Engine and Evidence-Grounded Post-Call Compliance Review System, can support relationship managers during customer conversations by interpreting questions and concerns across different languages, accents, and communication styles.

It can provide relevant prompts on considerations such as key product information and risk disclosures to complement relationship managers’ professional judgement and help them deliver clearer and more relevant customer conversations.

After each conversation, the solution can support an evidence-grounded review to assess whether key information was communicated clearly and fair dealing standards were met, providing an additional layer of governance for the bank.

It could also improve productivity by reducing manual translation and automating parts of the post-call review process, whilst providing insights for more targeted relationship manager coaching.

Relationship managers would remain accountable for the conversations and advice they provide, with AI complementing their professional judgement.

“Banking is built on trust, and every customer conversation matters,” said Leong Yung Chee, group chief financial officer at UOB.

“We want to apply AI with purpose, and we see potential for this solution to help our RMs better understand customers, navigate language and cultural nuances, and provide clearer, more relevant guidance,” Leong added.

MERaLiON supports multilingual processing and code-switching across 11 ASEAN languages, including Malay, Bahasa Indonesia, Thai, and Vietnamese, alongside English, Mandarin, Singlish, and traditional dialects such as Cantonese.

The model has achieved the lowest average word-error rate among open-source models across seven languages, according to UOB and A*STAR.

UOB said it will continue to assess how the model's capabilities can be applied safely and responsibly across its regional franchise.

data.title: Category A COE premium sinks to $130,100
data.description:
Larger and more powerful cars also got cheaper as 951 bids succeeded.

Singapore's Category A certificate of entitlement (COE) premium fell to $130,100 in the second November bidding exercise, down from $139,001 in the previous exercise, according to the Land Transport Authority.

COE premiums declined across three other categories, whilst the Open Category recorded a slight increase. The second bidding exercise closed on 18 November.

Category A received 1,464 bids, of which 1,130 were successful and 334 unsuccessful.

The category covers non-fully electric cars with engine capacities of up to 1,600cc and maximum power output of 97 kilowatts (kW), as well as fully electric cars with maximum power output of up to 110kW.

Category B, which covers larger and more powerful cars, recorded a premium of $125,600, down from $132,334. The category received 1,066 bids, of which 951 were successful.

For commercial vehicles and buses under Category C, the COE premium fell to $91,790, from $92,000, with 504 bids received.

Motorcycle premiums under Category D came in at $10,489, down from $10,689, with 635 bids received.

The Open Category premium edged up to $136,000 from $135,998, with 466 bids received.

data.title: CapitaLand Investment stresses leadership, staff buy-in to scale AI
data.description:
Over 8,000 staff use its AI work assistant across business operations. 

CapitaLand Investment Ltd is expanding its use of artificial intelligence (AI) across its businesses, but scaling the technology requires leadership support and changes in employee mindsets, according to its digital chief.

Wong Hwee Lim, Chief Digital & Technology Officer at CapitaLand Investment Ltd, said companies need to address workforce attitudes and secure senior management backing to move AI projects beyond experimentation.

“We first change the mindset,” Wong told the Singapore Business Review Technology Enterprise Summit on 12 November.

He also emphasised having support from the board and the senior leaders, noting the challenges of implementing AI beyond the proof-of-concept stage.

Wong outlined how CapitaLand Investment is applying AI across fund and investment management, commercial properties, lodging, and corporate operations.

In investment management, the company uses the solution to support market analysis, deal screening, and investment decisions.

Its ATLAS market intelligence platform, launched in April, provides access to more than 70,000 market reports and has reduced the time needed to compile market briefs from days to minutes.

For commercial property management, Wong highlighted the use of data to maximise rental yields, with AI-powered dashboards automating 80% of monthly asset reports and saving an estimated 1,300 man-hours annually.

Meanwhile, the company’s AI-powered retail assistant, Casey, has handled more than 370,000 customer chat sessions through the CapitaStar app and mall websites, reducing reliance on physical concierge desks and call centres.

In lodging, Wong highlighted the use of generative AI chatbots to handle customer inquiries, with the company’s Cubby chatbot supporting more than one million guest inquiries since 2023.

AI-powered dynamic pricing also generated up to $29.6m in additional revenue in FY2025, with the technology used across 105 properties.

Beyond customer-facing operations, the company has deployed AI assistants for internal workflows, including finance, human resources, IT support and cybersecurity.

More than 8,000 employees use its AI work assistant, whilst the company recorded 5,200 AI training attendances between January and mid-October.

data.title: Seatrium banks $12.2b order book across 35 projects
data.description:
Karpowership and Excelerate Energy booked 3 floating storage and regasification conversions.

Seatrium Limited reported a net order book of $12.2b across 35 projects as at 30 September, having secured $1.7b in new orders year-to-date.

Key contract wins included three floating storage and regasification unit conversions for Karpowership and Excelerate Energy, as well as floating production, storage, and offloading integration projects for SBM Offshore and MODEC.

The group also secured a contract to convert and integrate five next-generation Whale Class Powerships for Karpowership.

Seatrium is also progressing towards completing four offshore rigs for RigCo and has signed a letter of intent with Golar for a third floating liquefied natural gas project, with the definitive contract expected to be finalised by end-2026.

The group said operational performance remained steady in the third quarter, with revenue maintaining its run rate and gross margins improving from the first half.

Margin expansion was supported by a more favourable project mix, continued cost discipline, and cost savings from ongoing non-core divestments.

Annualised cost savings of more than $50m from completed divestments remain on track, whilst further divestment initiatives are expected to optimise the group's cost structure.

The group expects its net profit for financial year (FY) 2026 to be higher than in FY2025.

data.title: Experts flag execution risks in $1.82b Town Hall Link bid
data.description:
Consultants said the substantial office and infrastructure requirements narrowed the bidding field.

The two bids received for the Town Hall Link white site reflected developers’ caution towards large integrated projects and uncertainty over future suburban office demand, property consultants said.

A consortium comprising CapitaLand Development, Sing Holdings, Far East Organization and Sino Group submitted the highest bid of about $1.82b, equivalent to $910 psf per plot ratio.

The offer was nearly 39% above the second bid of approximately $1.31b, suggesting that the bidders held substantially different views about the value that could be extracted from the site.

The 3.72-hectare Jurong Lake District plot has a maximum gross floor area of about 2 million sq ft. It could yield approximately 1,200 homes, at least 40,000 sq m of office space and between 20,000 and 44,000 sq m of retail space.

Knight Frank Singapore Head of Research Leonard Tay said the two bids were within expectations because the project still represented a substantial undertaking despite being smaller than the Jurong Lake District master-developer site rejected in 2024.

He said developers would have weighed the site’s strategic position and transport connectivity against its infrastructure requirements and the untested popularity of suburban offices.

Corporate occupiers continued to prefer the Central Business District because of prestige, amenities and more equitable commuting times for employees, Tay said.

Knight Frank estimated that office users would be unlikely to pay more than $7.50 psf per month for space outside the Central Region, even in a new building with high-quality facilities.

The firm also cautioned that the $910 psf ppr bid, whilst 42% higher than the offer for the rejected master-developer site, could still fall below the government’s reserve price.

PropNex Head of Research and Content Wong Siew Ying described the top offer as measured rather than aggressive.

She said the significant capital commitment and need for expertise across residential, office and retail development naturally limited the tender to well-capitalised developers and consortiums.

The smaller plot and the government’s decision to take on more infrastructure and land-preparation work probably reduced bidders’ costs and risks compared with the earlier master site, she added.

PropNex expects the residential component to attract healthy demand from HDB upgraders in western Singapore and buyers drawn to the site’s future access to four MRT lines.

The agency estimated that the development could achieve an average selling price above $2,800 psf, supported by its connectivity, integrated format and the wider transformation of Jurong Lake District.

Huttons Asia CEO Mark Yip said the offer was likely the highest land-price quantum recorded for a white site outside the Central Area.

He said direct links to Jurong East MRT interchange and the future Jurong Lake District station, together with the retail podium and planned employment growth, would support its appeal to residents and investors.

Huttons also expects office-development risks to ease as Singapore’s supply of new office space peaks in 2028 and tapers over the following three years.

URA has not awarded the site. The authority said it would announce its decision after evaluating the bids.

data.title: A*STAR, finance institute to test trusted AI for banking
data.description:
UOB and Standard Chartered will participate in projects covering multilingual voice technology and model reliability.

A*STAR’s Institute of Advanced Intelligence and Computing and the Future of Finance Institute have agreed to develop and test artificial intelligence applications for Singapore’s financial sector.

Under a memorandum of understanding, the partners will identify priority research areas, publish findings and develop prototypes that translate AI research into practical financial-services applications.

The collaboration will initially focus on multilingual voice technology and improving the reliability of AI systems used by financial institutions.

The partners will explore the use of MERaLiON, A*STAR’s multilingual AI model, to process Singapore and Southeast Asia’s languages, accents and code-switching patterns.

The research could support more natural voice-to-text interactions in areas such as customer service and other financial workflows.

A*STAR and the institute will also work with financial institutions to evaluate AI systems, identify risks and performance gaps, and strengthen their reliability before deployment.

UOB and Standard Chartered Bank are the first financial institutions participating in the collaboration. They will provide practical use cases and industry expertise to help test and validate the models.

A*STAR IAIC Executive Director Su Yi said financial services required AI systems capable of strict accuracy, auditability and domain-specific precision, rather than conversational fluency alone.

Testing advanced models against actual operational workflows would help move trusted AI from research laboratories into critical financial infrastructure, he added.

Future of Finance Institute CEO Alan Lim said combining research and financial-industry expertise could accelerate responsible innovation and reinforce Singapore’s position in AI-enabled finance.

UOB said it would take a “governance by design” approach, incorporating security and reliability throughout the AI lifecycle.

Standard Chartered similarly said trust, governance and responsible deployment must remain central to adoption, particularly when voice-based AI models are introduced at scale.

data.title: Banks prepare for AI agents to take over the customer front end
data.description:
Four in five want AI and agentic assistance built into their main banking relationship.

Banking apps will remain but move into the background as customers’ AI agents take over how they discover and choose financial products, executives from Tencent, UOB, HSBC and Visa said at the Singapore FinTech Festival.

The shift could leave banks with fewer direct chances to earn customers’ attention and trust, and the panellists said institutions will need to rethink their channels, service design and how they handle customer consent.

“Customers are going to use their personal agents. There is no question about it,” said T.R. Ramachandran, head of products and solutions for Asia Pacific at Visa.

Ramachandran said the question isn’t whether customers use banks or agents, but where the journey begins and ends. He expects it will increasingly start with a customer’s agent discovering banking products, whilst the transaction still culminates in a bank’s app or digital channel.

Daniel Hong, vice president of Tencent Financial Technology, said banking apps will go the way of physical branches, still present but with a different role.

Apps will become the back end that handles the heavy lifting, whilst agents serve customers at the front end through natural language.

“Users don’t have to understand the menu, don’t have to figure out the buttons,” Hong said.

Customers already appear ready for the change. BCG research found 23% of its customers already use AI for their banking needs, and 75% want AI and agentic assistance built into their main banking relationship.

However, 82% said they would still want to approve every financial decision an agent makes, and the research found customers are less comfortable handing high-stakes, emotional decisions, such as mortgages and investment management, to AI.

Tencent’s answer is to let customers hand over control in stages. Its AI agent payment product, launched on WeChat this year, uses an isolated sub-account that only agents can spend from.

In the first phase, every agent payment needs the user’s approval and password. In the second, users only confirm their intent. In the third, agents act on their own within a set task and budget, such as planning a trip under US$2,000.

“The key to building trust in agents is not to ask for the trust, but to set up an environment so that the user can test, explore,” Hong said. Tencent is also working to make more mini programs agent-ready.

For Lee Zhu Kuang, managing director and head of UOB’s innovation group, the challenge is that both customers and banks will use agents, so institutions must decide how much authority each one gets.

“When we give the authority to an agent, it must reflect the customer intent, the impact of the decision as well as the risk that is being involved,” Lee said. After this, banks can create the guardrails around it.

Lee said banks can earn that delegation by giving customers positive, controlled experiences with agents, and by using agents to support people in complex, regulated or high-value decisions.

Banks can also stand out by redesigning the customer journey, not just the interface. UOB is exploring a conversational chatbot that helps customers find flights and hotels and pay with either their card or reward points.

Ultimately, Lee said, the relationship still matters.

“How do we make sure that the clients have someone or an institution to turn to when things go wrong?” Lee said.

Shayan Hazir, chief digital officer for Asia (excluding Hong Kong) and MENAT at HSBC, compared deciding which tasks to hand to agents with aircraft autopilot.

Machines handle certain tasks safely within guardrails, humans take over once thresholds are crossed, and everything is recorded. Hazir expects that balance to shift over time, just as autopilot evolved over a century.

Hazir argued that agents won’t reduce banks to a mechanical comparison. Instead, he said, this is the best opportunity yet for banks to differentiate, moving from hyper-personalisation to products built for a “segment of one,” where customers shape their own investment portfolios, facilities and rewards.

HSBC recently completed a business-to-business transaction using agents with two clients, a technology partner and a payments partner.

“It’s not human in the loop; it’s human judgment in design that needs to be the case,” Hazir said, adding that banks must work alongside regulators, such as the UK’s Financial Conduct Authority, which has issued principles on agentic commerce.

Ramachandran said trust in agentic payments rests on identity, authentication, consent and authorisation, plus a new element, signals, which capture whether an agent understood the customer’s intent. That matters for resolving disputes and stopping agents from going rogue.

Merchants also need to adapt, since online stores are built for humans, not machines. Ramachandran said many merchants are either letting all bots in or blocking them entirely.

Visa created its Trusted Agent Protocol so merchants can confirm an agent is who it says it is and has the customer’s consent.

“Like-minded players need to come together to create the right environment, the right sort of ecosystem, and the right guardrails,” Ramachandran said, adding that customer adoption is where agentic commerce can succeed enormously or fall flat on its face.
